weeks.title: The Lead-In: Tools, Repository, and the First Early Morning
weeks.theme: Three days before Week 1 begins. No theory yet — just the machine, the repository and the routine, set up so that Monday at 05:00 is spent learning and not installing things. The no-AI rule starts today.
weeks.deliverable: A working machine (Node LTS, Git, VS Code, a terminal you are comfortable in), a GitHub account with a profile photo and name, and a first commit in a practice repository.
weeks.milestone: Both lead-in days done at their scheduled times, including the 05:00 start on Friday. Sunday taken off properly.

weeks.title: The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand
weeks.theme: Nothing improves until it is measured honestly. This week you write down exactly where you are — including the parts that are embarrassing — and start the language work everything else sits on. No AI writes a line of code for you. That rule is the whole point.
weeks.deliverable: A public GitHub repository named backend-mastery containing LOG.md (one honest paragraph per day), week-01/ with every exercise you wrote by hand, and BASELINE.md recording your starting scores.
weeks.milestone: Six consecutive days with at least one commit. Baseline recorded for: LeetCode Easy solved unaided, JavaScript self-quiz score, and one honest sentence naming what you actually built in three years.

weeks.title: Scope, Closures, and the this Keyword
weeks.theme: Closures are the most common intermediate JavaScript interview question, and "this" is the one people three years in still get wrong. Both are the same idea: a function carries context with it. Get this week right and a whole category of questions stops being frightening.
weeks.deliverable: week-02/ containing a counter factory, a private-variable module, a memoisation wrapper, and a written explanation of the var-in-a-loop problem in your own words.
weeks.milestone: You can define a closure out loud, unaided, in one sentence, and produce a working example from a blank file in under five minutes.

weeks.title: Arrays, Objects, and Reading Errors Like an Engineer
weeks.theme: The array and object methods that appear in nearly every screening test, and the debugger — because the fastest way to look like a three-year engineer is to read a stack trace correctly instead of guessing.
weeks.deliverable: week-03/ containing an order-analysis script built with map/filter/reduce, and a written record of four bugs you introduced deliberately and fixed using only the debugger.
weeks.milestone: You can use reduce correctly from memory, and you can set a breakpoint, step into a call, and read the call stack without looking anything up.

weeks.title: The Event Loop, Promises, and the Paperwork Gate
weeks.theme: Async is where self-taught confidence collapses, and it is asked in every backend interview you will sit. In parallel the paperwork has to finish this week, because applications open on Monday and a gate that slips is a gate that never closes.
weeks.deliverable: CV version one as a real PDF, a rewritten LinkedIn profile, a GitHub profile with a README and no empty repositories, and week-04/ with hand-written promise exercises.
weeks.milestone: GATE — CV, LinkedIn and GitHub finished by Saturday 24 October. Not "nearly". A stranger can find you, read one page, and know what you do. And you can explain the event loop out loud in ninety seconds.

weeks.title: Git Properly, and the First Applications
weeks.theme: Applications open — three a week, every one tailored. Three is deliberately small: at this stage each application is a test of the CV, not a lottery ticket. The engineering half is Git, which you have used for three years and do not actually understand.
weeks.deliverable: Three tailored applications logged in APPLICATIONS.md, and a practice repository where you have created and resolved a merge conflict, rebased a branch, and recovered a lost commit from the reflog.
weeks.milestone: Three applications out. You can explain the difference between merge and rebase, and what git reset --hard actually destroys, without looking it up.

weeks.title: OOP and SOLID — The Shape NestJS Assumes
weeks.theme: NestJS is an opinionated object-oriented framework built on dependency injection. If classes, interfaces and inversion of control are vague to you, Nest will feel like magic and you will never debug it confidently. This week removes the magic before you meet it.
weeks.deliverable: week-06/ containing a small library system modelled in classes, refactored so the storage mechanism can be swapped without touching business logic, plus your own hand-written dependency-injection container in about thirty lines.
weeks.milestone: You can explain dependency inversion with an example from your own code, and you have written a DI container yourself — so Nest's providers will be obvious rather than magical.

weeks.title: TypeScript for Backend Engineers
weeks.theme: TypeScript is not optional at the tier you are targeting, and NestJS is built on its decorators and metadata. This week is types that carry weight — generics, narrowing, and the compiler settings that actually catch bugs — plus the decorator mechanics Nest depends on.
weeks.deliverable: The expense tracker ported to strict TypeScript with no any, plus a worked file demonstrating decorators and metadata reflection from first principles.
weeks.milestone: BLOCK I CLOSES. You can type a function, an object and a generic without help, you know what strict mode turns on, and you can explain what a decorator is at runtime.

weeks.title: The Node Runtime — Modules, npm, Process
weeks.theme: You have written server code for three years without knowing what the runtime does. This week is modules, resolution, the standard library and the process itself — the ground everything else stands on.
weeks.deliverable: week-08/ containing a three-module project built by hand in both CommonJS and ESM, a directory-walker using fs and path correctly, and a script that fails properly with a non-zero exit code.
weeks.milestone: You can explain module resolution, the difference between CommonJS and ESM, and what an unhandled rejection does to a Node process.

weeks.title: Node Internals — Event Loop Phases, Streams, Buffers
weeks.theme: The week that separates you from every other candidate who says "Node is non-blocking" and cannot go further. Libuv phases, the thread pool, streams and backpressure, and what a Buffer actually is.
weeks.deliverable: week-09/ containing a measured demonstration of a blocked event loop, a stream pipeline that processes a file larger than memory, and a written explanation of backpressure in your own words.
weeks.milestone: You can name the event loop phases in order, explain what runs in the thread pool and what does not, and demonstrate backpressure with code you wrote.

weeks.title: Express — Routing, Middleware, the Request Lifecycle
weeks.theme: Express is small enough to understand completely, and understanding it completely is what lets you answer the most common backend interview question at this level: what happens between the request arriving and the response leaving.
weeks.deliverable: week-10/ containing an Express server with a hand-written middleware stack — request id, logging, timing, body limit, auth check, central error handler — every one written by you, and a diagram of the request lifecycle drawn by you.
weeks.milestone: You can draw the path of a request through an Express app from memory, including where errors go and why middleware order is not cosmetic.

weeks.title: REST API Design a Reviewer Would Approve
weeks.theme: Anyone can make an endpoint return JSON. This week is the decisions a reviewer looks at: resource naming, status codes, pagination, filtering, idempotency, versioning, and what your API does when the client sends nonsense.
weeks.deliverable: The Project 1 API with two resources, full CRUD, pagination, filtering, a single documented error shape, and an OpenAPI document that matches the implementation.
weeks.milestone: You can defend every status code your API returns, and explain cursor versus offset pagination and when each breaks.

weeks.title: Validation, Error Handling, Logging
weeks.theme: The unglamorous week that separates a project that looks like a tutorial from one that looks like production. None of it is hard and all of it is visible to a reviewer within thirty seconds of opening your repository.
weeks.deliverable: Project 1 with schema validation on every input, a real error taxonomy with custom error classes, and structured logging where a request id flows through every log line for one request.
weeks.milestone: You can trace a single request end to end through your logs by its id, and you can explain the difference between an operational error and a programmer error.

weeks.title: Deploy It — The API Goes Public
weeks.theme: A deployed thing you can link to changes every conversation you have from here on. It is not finished and that is the point: deploy early, deploy badly, learn what breaks, and then have a URL on your CV for the remaining thirty-seven weeks.
weeks.deliverable: PROJECT 1 API DEPLOYED at a public URL over HTTPS, with a health check, environment-based configuration, and a README a stranger can follow.
weeks.milestone: ANCHOR — the API is reachable from the public internet on Saturday 26 December. Application quota rises to five a week because the CV now points at something running.

weeks.title: SQL I — Selects, Joins, Thinking in Sets
weeks.theme: You have written SQL for three years and most of it was generated. SQL is the highest-return subject in this book: asked in almost every interview, testable in fifteen minutes, and being genuinely good at it is rare enough to be a differentiator.
weeks.deliverable: A seeded PostgreSQL practice database of five related tables and a few thousand rows, plus forty solved exercises written by hand with no AI and no copied answers.
weeks.milestone: You can write a three-table join with grouping and a having clause from a blank editor, first try, without looking up the syntax.

weeks.title: SQL II — Window Functions and the Hard Queries
weeks.theme: The second SQL week, and the one that makes you unusual. Window functions are asked at tier 2, rarely known at tier 4, and they turn a category of "impossible without application code" questions into four lines.
weeks.deliverable: week-15/ containing thirty more solved exercises covering window functions, ranking, running totals, gaps and islands, and set operations.
weeks.milestone: You can produce a per-group top-N query and a running total with a window function, from memory, and explain what the frame clause does.

weeks.title: Schema Design and Normalization
weeks.theme: Design questions separate three-year engineers from each other. Anyone can query a schema someone else designed. This week is designing one that does not have to be rescued in eighteen months.
weeks.deliverable: A designed, documented and migrated schema for Project 1 — entities, relationships, keys, constraints — with a written justification for every denormalisation you chose.
weeks.milestone: Given a described business problem you can produce a normalised schema on paper in twenty minutes and defend each decision.

weeks.title: PostgreSQL in Depth
weeks.theme: PostgreSQL specifically, not "a database". Types that prevent bugs, JSONB for the genuinely schemaless parts, psql instead of a GUI, and the features that make Postgres the default answer at the companies you are targeting.
weeks.deliverable: Project 1 using correct Postgres types throughout, one justified JSONB column with an index on it, and a written note on every type choice you changed and why.
weeks.milestone: You can use psql without a GUI, and you can explain why timestamptz and numeric exist and what goes wrong without them.

weeks.title: Indexes and Query Plans
weeks.theme: The single most valuable week in the plan for your market position. Very few three-year candidates in this market can honestly say "I read query plans". After this week you can, with numbers from your own project.
weeks.deliverable: A written before-and-after for five queries you indexed, with the EXPLAIN ANALYZE output for each and the timing difference.
weeks.milestone: You can read an EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan, say which line is the problem, and predict whether an index will help before you create it.

weeks.title: Transactions and Concurrency — and AI Comes Back
weeks.theme: Transactions separate a developer from an engineer in a backend interview. Two users buying the last item at the same moment is a question you will be asked, and the answer is not "I would check the stock first". Also: on Monday, AI returns as a reviewer.
weeks.deliverable: week-19/ containing a demonstrated lost-update race condition and three different correct fixes, each with the SQL and a written explanation of its trade-off.
weeks.milestone: ANCHOR — AI unlocked on Monday 1 February, as reviewer and teacher, never author. And you can describe a race condition you personally reproduced.

weeks.title: ORMs — Prisma and TypeORM
weeks.theme: Every team you interview with uses an ORM, and the useful answer to "why not raw SQL" is one you can only give having done both. You have written six weeks of SQL by hand; now learn what an ORM buys and what it quietly costs.
weeks.deliverable: Project 1 on Prisma, with three queries deliberately left in raw SQL and a comment on each saying why, plus a written comparison of Prisma and TypeORM from having used both.
weeks.milestone: You can name three things an ORM makes worse, not just three it makes better. And you can reproduce and fix an N+1 query on demand.

weeks.title: MongoDB and Modelling Without Joins
weeks.theme: NoSQL is not "SQL but easier", it is a different modelling discipline: you design around your queries instead of around your entities. Knowing when a document store is genuinely right — and saying so honestly — is worth more in an interview than knowing its syntax.
weeks.deliverable: A second copy of one Project 1 domain modelled in MongoDB, with the aggregation pipeline equivalents of three of your SQL reports, and a written argument for which store you would actually choose.
weeks.milestone: You can explain embedding versus referencing with a rule for choosing, and you can write an aggregation pipeline with $match, $group and $lookup from memory.

weeks.title: Replication, Partitioning, Sharding — and the Block Close
weeks.theme: The scaling vocabulary. You will not shard anything this year, and you will be asked about it, because the question tests whether you understand the trade-offs rather than whether you have operated one.
weeks.deliverable: A working local replica of your Postgres database with reads served from it, one partitioned table with a demonstrated pruning benefit, and a written scaling path for Project 1 from one server to many.
weeks.milestone: BLOCK III CLOSES — ANCHOR: Project 1 has a complete, indexed, transactional data layer across SQL and NoSQL by Saturday 27 February. You can explain replication lag and why it breaks read-after-write.

weeks.title: NestJS Fundamentals — Modules, Controllers, Providers, DI
weeks.theme: The architecture, and why it exists. Nest is Angular's structure applied to the server: modules that declare what they own, providers resolved by a container, and controllers that do nothing but translate HTTP. You built a crude version of this in week 6; now see it done properly.
weeks.deliverable: PROJECT 2 started — the Nest skeleton of your Project 1 domain, with two feature modules, controllers, services and repositories, wired by DI, and a written comparison against your own week-6 container.
weeks.milestone: You can explain what the Nest DI container does at startup, what a provider token is, and why a circular dependency between two modules happens — without calling any of it magic.

weeks.title: The Request Pipeline — Pipes, Guards, Interceptors, Filters
weeks.theme: Nest's request pipeline is Express middleware with names and ordering guarantees. Knowing the exact order — middleware, guards, interceptors, pipes, handler, interceptors again, filters — is the single most asked Nest interview question.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 with a validation pipe on every DTO, a guard protecting one route, a logging interceptor adding timing, and a global exception filter producing your standard error shape.
weeks.milestone: You can draw the Nest request pipeline in order from memory and say what each stage is for and what it must not do.

weeks.title: The Nest Data Layer — TypeORM, Prisma, Transactions
weeks.theme: Connecting Block III to Block IV. The repository pattern Nest assumes, migrations that run in CI, and transactions that span services — which is the part every tutorial skips and every real system needs.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 on a real database with entities, migrations, a repository layer behind interfaces, and one multi-service operation wrapped in a single transaction.
weeks.milestone: You can explain how a transaction spans two services in Nest without passing a connection object through every method signature.

weeks.title: Authentication and Authorisation in Nest
weeks.theme: Auth is the most commonly implemented and most commonly implemented-badly part of a backend, and a favourite interview subject because the wrong answers are so recognisable. Build it properly once, in Nest, and understand every trade-off you chose.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 with registration, login, refresh, logout, role-based authorisation on at least two routes, and a written justification of the session-versus-token decision.
weeks.milestone: You can explain why a JWT in localStorage is a risk, what refresh-token rotation solves, and how you log a user out of a stateless system. Nobody at this level should be guessing here.

weeks.title: Testing — Unit, Integration, End to End
weeks.theme: You have never written a test. At tier 2 that is disqualifying, and it is the easiest gap in this book to close: one week of real tests on a project you already understand changes how your repository reads to a reviewer.
weeks.deliverable: A real test suite on Project 2 — unit tests on business logic, integration tests on the repository layer against a throwaway database, e2e tests on every endpoint — running green from a clean checkout.
weeks.milestone: The suite runs green from empty, covers every endpoint at least once including failure paths, and you can explain what you deliberately chose not to test.

weeks.title: GraphQL and WebSockets in Nest
weeks.theme: Two protocols beyond REST that appear constantly in job descriptions at this tier. Neither is hard once you have REST properly; both are asked about, and having shipped each once is the difference between an opinion and an answer.
weeks.deliverable: A GraphQL layer over part of the Project 2 domain with a solved N+1 via DataLoader, and a WebSocket gateway pushing live updates to connected clients.
weeks.milestone: You can explain the N+1 problem in GraphQL specifically and how DataLoader batches it, and you can say when WebSockets are the wrong choice.

weeks.title: The Work That Happens Later — Uploads, Email, Cron, Microservices
weeks.theme: The last Nest week. Everything a real service does besides answer requests: accept files, send email, run scheduled work, and talk to other services. Plus Nest's microservice transports, so you can speak about distributed systems from having touched one.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 with pre-signed direct file upload, transactional email, two scheduled jobs that are safe to run on multiple instances, and one module extracted into a separate microservice.
weeks.milestone: BLOCK IV CLOSES. You can explain why a cron job on three instances runs three times and the three ways to stop it — which is a question that catches most candidates.

weeks.title: Redis and Caching Strategies
weeks.theme: Caching is easy to add and hard to invalidate, and "cache invalidation" jokes are told by people who have never had to do it. This week is Redis as a real data structure server, and caching as a decision with a written invalidation strategy.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 with a measured cache on its most expensive read path, a written invalidation strategy, and Redis-backed sessions and WebSocket fan-out.
weeks.milestone: You can name four caching strategies and say which one you used and why, and you can describe a cache stampede and how you would prevent it.

weeks.title: Queues, Workers and Message Brokers
weeks.theme: The moment a request does work the user should not wait for, you need a queue — and the moment you have a queue you need to think about retries, failures and ordering. This is the backbone of every serious backend and it is where system design interviews go.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 with a real job queue and a separate worker process, retries with backoff, a dead-letter queue, and one event-driven flow where a write publishes an event that two handlers consume.
weeks.milestone: You can explain at-least-once versus at-most-once delivery, why idempotent consumers are mandatory, and what a dead-letter queue is for.

weeks.title: Rate Limiting, API Gateways and Resilience
weeks.theme: Protecting a service from its callers, and from its own dependencies. Rate limiting, circuit breakers, timeouts and retries — the difference between a service that degrades and one that falls over and takes its neighbours with it.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 with a Redis-backed distributed rate limiter, timeouts and a circuit breaker on every outbound call, and a written note on what the service does when each dependency is unavailable.
weeks.milestone: You can explain the difference between a fixed window, a sliding window and a token bucket, and why an in-memory rate limiter is wrong the moment you run two instances.

weeks.title: Ship Project 2
weeks.theme: A finished project is one a stranger can use, understand and evaluate without you in the room. This week is the last ten per cent, which is always more than ten per cent — and at the end you have two shipped backend services, which is two more than most candidates.
weeks.deliverable: PROJECT 2 LIVE — deployed, documented, with a demo account, an architecture diagram, a two-minute demo video, and the measured numbers from weeks 18, 28, 30 and 31 in the README.
weeks.milestone: ANCHOR — Project 2 live by Saturday 15 May. A NestJS service with a real data layer, auth, queues, caching, real-time and tests, running at a public URL.

weeks.title: Linux and the Shell
weeks.theme: Every server you will touch is Linux and every pipeline is a shell script. You have avoided both for three years. One week to stop being a tourist on the command line.
weeks.deliverable: week-34/ containing a backup script that dumps a database, compresses, rotates anything older than seven days, logs every step and exits non-zero on failure — plus a successful restore from it.
weeks.milestone: You can diagnose a Linux box over SSH with no GUI: what is listening, what is eating memory, what filled the disk, what the logs say.

weeks.title: Docker and Docker Compose
weeks.theme: Containers are the vocabulary of every infrastructure conversation you will have. The goal is not memorising commands — it is understanding images, layers and networking well enough to debug when it does not work.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 fully containerised — a multi-stage Dockerfile under 200MB running as a non-root user, and a compose file bringing up API, worker, Postgres and Redis with one command.
weeks.milestone: A stranger can clone Project 2 and run the whole stack with one command, and you can explain the difference between an image and a container without hedging.

weeks.title: Nginx, TLS, DNS and the Network
weeks.theme: What sits in front of your service, and how a request actually reaches it. Reverse proxying, certificates, DNS and the network layer — all of it asked about, most of it never learned properly by people who deploy to a platform that hides it.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 behind Nginx on a domain you own, with a real certificate that auto-renews, gzip, correct proxy headers, and a written trace of a request from DNS lookup to response.
weeks.milestone: You can explain what happens between typing a URL and receiving a response, including DNS, TCP, TLS and the proxy — end to end, from memory.

weeks.title: CI/CD with GitHub Actions
weeks.theme: Tests nobody runs are documentation. This week the tests run on every push, the image builds in the pipeline, and deployment stops being something you do by hand at eleven at night.
weeks.deliverable: A GitHub Actions pipeline on Project 2: lint, test against a service database, build and push the image, deploy on merge to main — with branch protection that blocks a red build.
weeks.milestone: A pull request with a failing test cannot be merged, and deployment happens on merge rather than by hand.

weeks.title: Jenkins
weeks.theme: A large number of Pakistani employers run Jenkins, often self-hosted and inherited. GitHub Actions teaches you pipelines; Jenkins teaches you the version of pipelines that a real company asks you to maintain. Knowing both is a hiring advantage.
weeks.deliverable: A Jenkins instance running in Docker with a declarative Jenkinsfile in the Project 2 repository — checkout, install, lint, test against a database, build the image, deploy on main — plus credentials handled properly and one shared library function.
weeks.milestone: BLOCK VI CLOSES. The same pipeline exists twice, in Actions and in Jenkins, and you can compare them from experience rather than opinion.

weeks.title: AWS Foundations — IAM, EC2, S3
weeks.theme: You have the certificate and have never built anything. This week gives it evidence: identity, a server you configured, and object storage wired into your own application.
weeks.deliverable: An AWS account locked down with MFA and least-privilege users, a billing alarm, Project 2 running on EC2, and S3 handling uploads through pre-signed URLs with public access blocked.
weeks.milestone: You can explain the difference between an IAM user, a role and a policy, and why an application should use a role rather than an access key.

weeks.title: Networking and Managed Data — VPC, RDS, ELB, Auto Scaling
weeks.theme: The part of AWS that is actually architecture. A private network, a managed database that is not reachable from the internet, a load balancer in front, and a group that replaces an instance when it dies.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 on a VPC you designed — public and private subnets, RDS in private with no public access, an application load balancer in front, and an auto-scaling group of at least two instances.
weeks.milestone: You can draw your own VPC from memory and explain the path of a packet from the internet to the database and back.

weeks.title: Containers and Serverless on AWS — ECS, EKS, Lambda, SQS
weeks.theme: Where your Docker work meets the cloud. ECS for running containers without operating Kubernetes, enough EKS to hold the conversation, Lambda for the work that suits it, and SQS because your queue should not depend on one Redis box.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 running on ECS Fargate — API and worker as separate services behind the load balancer, secrets from Secrets Manager, and one queue moved to SQS with a dead-letter queue.
weeks.milestone: You can explain when you would choose ECS over EKS over Lambda, in terms of what each costs you rather than what each is called.

weeks.title: Observability — CloudWatch, Prometheus, Grafana
weeks.theme: You cannot operate what you cannot see. Logs you can search, metrics that mean something, dashboards that answer a question, and exactly one alarm that wakes you up — because an alert nobody acts on trains you to ignore alerts.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 exporting application metrics to Prometheus, a Grafana dashboard answering four real questions, logs searchable in CloudWatch, and one alarm on a symptom that reaches your phone.
weeks.milestone: BLOCK VII CLOSES. You can answer "how do you know the service is healthy?" by opening a dashboard rather than describing an intention.

weeks.title: LLM Fundamentals and Prompt Engineering
weeks.theme: Not a course on AI. A working understanding of tokens, context, cost and failure modes, so that Project 3 is engineering rather than incantation — and so you answer AI questions like a backend engineer rather than a user.
weeks.deliverable: PROJECT3.md with a one-paragraph scope and a chosen document set, plus a working API integration with token accounting, a hard cost ceiling, retries and a measured cost per request.
weeks.milestone: You can state Project 3's cost per thousand requests, and explain what a token is and why a context window is a constraint rather than a feature.

weeks.title: Embeddings, Vector Search and RAG
weeks.theme: Retrieval is a search problem wearing new clothes, and the engineering is the unglamorous half: chunking, indexing, and evaluating whether what you retrieved was any good. The evaluation set is what makes this engineering.
weeks.deliverable: A working retrieval pipeline on pgvector with an evaluation set of at least twenty question-and-expected-source pairs, and a measured retrieval accuracy you can quote.
weeks.milestone: You can explain what an embedding is without hand-waving, and you have a number for how often your retrieval returns the right source.

weeks.title: Agents, MCP, and Ship Project 3
weeks.theme: Where tool-calling fits and where it does not, the protocol that is becoming the standard way to expose tools to models, and then the same shipping discipline as the first two projects.
weeks.deliverable: PROJECT 3 LIVE — deployed with a demo account, guardrails and cost caps, a README stating measured retrieval accuracy and cost per query, and one MCP server exposing a Project 2 capability as a tool.
weeks.milestone: ANCHOR — Project 3 live by Saturday 7 August, with measured retrieval quality. Three shipped backend services, all linkable, all explainable line by line.

weeks.title: HTML, CSS and Tailwind — Enough to Not Be Helpless
weeks.theme: One week on markup and layout. The goal is a clean, responsive page you built yourself, not a design career. Semantic HTML and flexbox will carry ninety per cent of what you ever need.
weeks.deliverable: A responsive, accessible admin page for Project 2 built in Tailwind — navigation, a data table, a form — that works on a phone.
weeks.milestone: You can build a two-column responsive layout from a blank file and explain what semantic HTML gives you beyond neatness.

weeks.title: React — Enough to Demo Your Own APIs
weeks.theme: One week of React. Components, state, data fetching, forms, and an authenticated route. Enough to show your backends working and to answer React questions without bluffing.
weeks.deliverable: A working admin interface for Project 2 — list, detail, create, edit, login, protected routes — reading live data, with loading, error and empty states handled everywhere.
weeks.milestone: BLOCK IX CLOSES. You can demo all three services through an interface you built, and no screen renders undefined.

weeks.title: Data Structures, Algorithms and Forty Problems
weeks.theme: Not competitive programming. The specific patterns that appear in Pakistani technical rounds, solved unaided, out loud, under a clock — with forty-seven weeks of Saturday drills already behind you.
weeks.deliverable: Forty problems solved unaided across the week, each with a written note on its pattern and complexity, plus a one-page pattern sheet in your own words.
weeks.milestone: ANCHOR approaches — forty problems unaided. Given an unseen medium problem you can name a plausible pattern within two minutes.

dsa.topic: Full review — 40 problems across the week

weeks.title: System Design, and Mock Loops With Real People
weeks.theme: At three years you are not expected to design a global system. You are expected to reason out loud, ask about scale before designing for it, and justify a cache or a replica. You have built all of it — this week is learning to perform it.
weeks.deliverable: Four designs produced under a clock on one page each, a written script for the first five minutes of any design round, and at least three mock interviews with real people with written feedback.
weeks.milestone: ANCHOR — first mock with a real person on Monday 30 August. Three mocks done by Saturday, feedback written down and acted on.

weeks.title: Offers, Negotiation, and the Honest Accounting
weeks.theme: Two jobs this week. Convert whatever is in the pipeline, and decide honestly what happens next — because the plan closing is not the same as the search closing, and the worst outcome is drifting back to where you started.
weeks.deliverable: A written final accounting — every number from BASELINE.md then and now, the full application funnel — and a concrete plan for the next eight weeks with dates on it.
weeks.milestone: DEADLINE — the plan closes on Saturday 11 September 2027. The accounting is written, the next eight weeks are planned, and nothing is left vague.

days.weekTitle: The Lead-In: Tools, Repository, and the First Early Morning
days.focus: Set up the machine — before anything else

tasks.text: Install Node.js LTS, Git and VS Code. Configure git user.name and user.email. From a terminal, check that node -v, npm -v and git --version all work. Create a folder called practice, run git init, add a README.md with one line, and commit it. No AI — use the official install pages.

Log in to GitHub (create an account if needed). Set a real profile photo, your full name and your city. This profile is going to be read by recruiters in a month, so it starts looking professional today.

days.weekTitle: The Lead-In: Tools, Repository, and the First Early Morning
days.focus: Walk through the plan, then a first warm-up

tasks.text: Skim Phase 0 Chapter 1 (How to Use This Book) — you read it properly on Monday. Then go through the Plan tab: read the Phase 12 overview chapter (The Plan) end to end, and look through Weeks 1–4 day by day. Then put the plan's times in your phone calendar as recurring events — 05:00–06:30 and 13:00–13:30 on weekdays, 08:00–13:00 on Saturdays.

DSA warm-up, no AI: create a LeetCode account and solve two Easy array problems (for example Two Sum and Contains Duplicate). Take up to twenty-five minutes each. This is not the baseline — that is on Tuesday. It only gets the rust off.

First review: write down which setup steps were harder than they should have been, and what time you actually woke up on Friday. Then read Phase 0 Chapter 7 (The Whole Day): set up your prayer-times app, gym split and phone rules, and book the urologist and dermatologist from its 30-day health checklist. Get everything for Monday ready tonight — the laptop, the chapter open, the alarm set. Sunday is off.

days.weekTitle: The Lead-In: Tools, Repository, and the First Early Morning
The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand
days.focus: The audit — write down where you really are

tasks.text: Read Phase 0 Chapter 1 (How to Use This Book) and Chapter 2 (The Mission) end to end. Then start Chapter 4 (The AI Dependency Problem) — it is about you, and it is not an insult.

Open BASELINE.md. Write three things: your current title and salary, the title and salary you want by 11 September 2027, and one honest paragraph naming what you personally built in three years versus what an AI built for you. Nobody else reads this. Lying here costs you the plan.

days.weekTitle: The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand
days.focus: The coding baseline — three problems, no help

tasks.text: Create the GitHub repository backend-mastery (public). Add LOG.md and BASELINE.md, commit, push. Then the coding baseline: three LeetCode Easy problems, twenty-five minutes each, no AI, no searching beyond language documentation. Record how many you finished unaided. If the answer is zero, write zero.

List ten target companies with backend teams. Start with: Arbisoft, Systems Ltd, 10Pearls, VentureDive, Devsinc, Tkxel, Motive, Careem, Folio3, Confiz. Find each careers page URL and write it into TARGETS.md.

days.weekTitle: The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand
days.focus: Values, types, and what === is really doing

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 1 (JavaScript) — "Chapter Overview" and "Beginner Theory" in full. Focus on primitives versus objects, and why == and === behave differently. Write notes in your own words in LOG.md, not copied sentences.
Create a plain-text master CV file. List every project you touched in three years, one line each: what it did, what you did on it, and one number if you can find one.

days.weekTitle: The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand

tasks.text: No AI: write ten small functions that each demonstrate one type-coercion rule. Predict the output of each before running it. Every wrong prediction is the lesson — write down why you were wrong. Commit it.
Read Phase 10 Chapter 1 (Speaking About Your Work). Write a four-sentence answer to "What do you do at your current job?" Say it aloud three times. Record yourself once and listen back.

days.weekTitle: The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand
days.focus: Name the habit you are here to break

tasks.text: Finish Phase 0 Chapter 4. Then write in LOG.md the three specific things you have reached for AI to do in the last month that you could not do alone. Be exact — "wrote the SQL for the report screen", not "helped with backend". Those three lines are your syllabus.
Write your LinkedIn headline and About section as a draft. Headline formula: the role you want (Backend Engineer), your core stack, one proof point. Not "aspiring" anything.

days.weekTitle: The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: a command-line contact book in plain Node — add, list, search, delete, saved to a JSON file. No framework, no packages. If you get stuck, read documentation and sit with it. This is the muscle.

DSA drill — read Phase 1 Chapter 13 (DSA Interview Patterns), Chapter Overview and the ladder table. Then this week's set: arrays and hashing, timed, no help. Every Saturday from here follows that ladder, and the app shows the week's topic.
Weekly review in LOG.md: how many days did I hit both blocks? Did I break the no-AI rule, and where? What do I understand today that I did not on Monday? Then read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand
Scope, Closures, and the this Keyword

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 1 — scope and hoisting. Learn the difference between var, let and const in terms of where the binding lives, not just "var is old". Predict the output of five hoisting puzzles before running them.
Rewrite the three strongest CV lines as achievement bullets: verb, what you did, result. No adjectives. If you cannot find a number, say what changed instead.

days.weekTitle: Scope, Closures, and the this Keyword

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 1 — closures. A closure is a function that remembers the variables around it after the outer function has finished. Read until you can say that sentence in your own words and mean it, then write it in LOG.md without looking.
Read Phase 0 Chapter 3 (Beginner to Mastery Path). Write which of the five levels you are honestly at for JavaScript, and what evidence you have for that answer.

days.weekTitle: Scope, Closures, and the this Keyword

tasks.text: No AI: build a counter factory, a private-variable module, and a memoisation wrapper. Three classic closure exercises, blank file each time. Commit all three.
Find five more target companies that are NOT in the famous ten — smaller product companies and credible software houses with real backend teams. Add them to TARGETS.md.

days.weekTitle: Scope, Closures, and the this Keyword

tasks.text: No AI: loop over an array with var inside a setTimeout and explain in LOG.md why it prints what it prints. Then fix it three ways — let, an IIFE, a bound argument — and explain why each works.
Read Phase 0 Chapter 5 (The Operating System). Write one paragraph on which current habit this plan asks you to break, and which one you expect to fail at first.

days.weekTitle: Scope, Closures, and the this Keyword

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 1 — the "this" sections. Learn the four binding rules and why arrow functions have no this of their own. No AI: write one example of each rule and predict the output before running.
Rewrite the remaining CV bullets in the achievement format. Content first, design later.

days.weekTitle: Scope, Closures, and the this Keyword
days.focus: Build something with closures in it

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: extend the contact book with an undo stack and a simple event system (on/emit). Both are closure exercises wearing a coat. No packages.
Drill: three LeetCode Easy, timed, no help. Then explain one solution out loud in English as if to an interviewer. Record it.
Weekly review. Did the dawn block hold five days out of five? Where did it slip, and what caused the slip? Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Scope, Closures, and the this Keyword
Arrays, Objects, and Reading Errors Like an Engineer

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 1 — array methods. Write each of map, filter and reduce yourself from scratch as a plain function before using the built-in. That is the exercise that makes reduce stop being scary.
Read Phase 11 Chapter 2 (The CV That Gets Read), first half. Note every rule your current CV breaks.

days.weekTitle: Arrays, Objects, and Reading Errors Like an Engineer

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 1 — objects, destructuring, spread. No AI: write five functions that pull values cleanly out of a deeply nested object. Learn what optional chaining actually protects you from.
Phase 10 Chapter 1 — finish it. Rewrite your four-sentence "what do you do" answer using what the chapter says about concrete detail.

days.weekTitle: Arrays, Objects, and Reading Errors Like an Engineer

tasks.text: No AI: from twenty fake order objects produce total revenue, revenue per customer, the top three customers, and a lookup map keyed by id. Use reduce at least twice. Commit it.
Rewrite your CV summary — three lines, no clichés, naming your stack and your years. Delete every "passionate", "hardworking" and "team player".

days.weekTitle: Arrays, Objects, and Reading Errors Like an Engineer

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 1 — the "Debugging" section. Breakpoints, step over versus step into, the call stack. Practise on yesterday's order script until you stop using console.log as your only tool.
Write a five-sentence explanation of what a stack trace is, aimed at a junior. Read it aloud. If you cannot explain it simply, you have not learned it.

days.weekTitle: Arrays, Objects, and Reading Errors Like an Engineer
days.focus: Break it on purpose, fix it with the debugger

tasks.text: No AI: break the order script four ways — undefined property, wrong type, off-by-one, async result used too early — and fix each using only the debugger and the stack trace. Write what each error message actually told you.
Read Phase 1 Chapter 10 (Clean Code) — naming and function length only. Rename every variable in this week's code you would be embarrassed to explain in a review.

days.weekTitle: Arrays, Objects, and Reading Errors Like an Engineer

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: a small expense tracker in plain Node — add, list by category, monthly totals, biggest category, JSON storage. Use the array methods deliberately, not accidentally.
Drill: four LeetCode Easy, timed, no help. Array-heavy ones. Compare the count against week 1.
Weekly review. Name the three JavaScript ideas you now hold that you did not three weeks ago, and the one you are still faking. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Arrays, Objects, and Reading Errors Like an Engineer
The Event Loop, Promises, and the Paperwork Gate
days.focus: The event loop — why JavaScript does not block

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 7 (Asynchronous Programming) — the event loop. Call stack, task queue, microtask queue. Draw it on paper. Then predict the output of five setTimeout/Promise ordering puzzles before running them.
Phase 11 Chapter 2 — finish it. Then build CV draft one: one page, standard headings, no columns, no photo, no skill bars. Structure only this pass.

days.weekTitle: The Event Loop, Promises, and the Paperwork Gate
days.focus: Callbacks, and why they became a problem

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 7 — callbacks and the error-first convention. No AI: write a three-level nested callback chain, feel it, then write down exactly what is unpleasant about it. You need to have felt this to explain why promises exist.
CV pass two: every bullet starts with a verb, every bullet says what changed. Cut anything you could not defend for sixty seconds. One page, hard limit.

days.weekTitle: The Event Loop, Promises, and the Paperwork Gate

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 7 — promises. Then, no AI: write your own tiny promise-like class with then and catch. It will not be spec-compliant and that is fine. Building it is what makes .then() stop being magic.
LinkedIn: headline, About, experience entries. Same rules as the CV. Add your GitHub link. Turn on "open to work" for recruiters only.

days.weekTitle: The Event Loop, Promises, and the Paperwork Gate

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 7 — Promise.all, allSettled, race, any. No AI: write one realistic use for each, then a retry-with-backoff helper from a blank file. Commit it.
GitHub profile: add a profile README saying who you are and what you are building. Archive every empty or abandoned repository. Pin backend-mastery.

days.weekTitle: The Event Loop, Promises, and the Paperwork Gate
days.focus: async/await, and the errors it hides

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 7 — async/await. Learn what await does to the function around it, and why a missing try/catch in an async function is the most common production bug in Node. No AI: convert your retry helper to async/await.
Read Phase 11 Chapter 8 (Portfolio and Personal Brand). Export CV version one to PDF as FirstnameLastname-CV.pdf. Send it to yourself and open it on a phone.

days.weekTitle: The Event Loop, Promises, and the Paperwork Gate

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: a script that calls three public APIs in parallel, handles partial failure with allSettled, retries on timeout, and prints a combined result. The async chapter as a working thing.
GATE CHECK. CV, LinkedIn and GitHub side by side. All three finished today. If one is not, finish it now — the rest of the plan assumes it is done.
Weekly review. Then: explain the event loop out loud, timed, ninety seconds, recorded. If you cannot, that is Monday's dawn block. Read next week ahead — applications open Monday.

days.weekTitle: The Event Loop, Promises, and the Paperwork Gate
Git Properly, and the First Applications

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 11 (Git) — the object model. Commits, trees, blobs, refs. Understand that a branch is a moving pointer to a commit and most of Git stops being frightening.

APPLICATIONS OPEN. Read Phase 11 Chapter 3 (Applying Without Wasting Shots), then send one application from TARGETS.md. Tailor the CV summary line to it. Log company, role, date, link and channel in APPLICATIONS.md.

days.weekTitle: Git Properly, and the First Applications

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 11 — branching and merging. In a throwaway repository: create a conflict deliberately, resolve it by hand, and write in LOG.md what the conflict markers actually mean.
Write the cover note you will reuse: four sentences, naming the company and one specific thing about them. Not a letter — something a recruiter reads in twelve seconds.

days.weekTitle: Git Properly, and the First Applications

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 11 — rebase, interactive rebase, and the golden rule about rewriting shared history. Squash this week's commits into three meaningful ones on a practice branch.
Second application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Git Properly, and the First Applications

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 11 — reset, revert, stash, reflog. Deliberately lose a commit with reset --hard and recover it from the reflog. Knowing this is the difference between a bad afternoon and a lost day.
Write a sixty-second spoken answer to "Why are you looking to leave your current job?" that is honest and does not criticise your employer.

days.weekTitle: Git Properly, and the First Applications

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 12 (GitHub) — pull requests, reviews, issues. Open a PR against your own backend-mastery repository, review it as if you were someone else, and leave three real comments.
Third application, tailored, logged. Then review the week's three: which did you tailor properly, and which did you send because the slot was open?

days.weekTitle: Git Properly, and the First Applications

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: a promise pool that runs N async jobs with a concurrency limit, then use it to fetch fifty URLs five at a time. This is a real interview question at the companies you are targeting.
Drill: three LeetCode Easy and one Medium, timed, no help. The Medium will probably beat you. Write where you got stuck — that is the useful output, not the solve.
Weekly review. Applications sent: 3. Responses: record honestly. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Git Properly, and the First Applications
OOP and SOLID — The Shape NestJS Assumes

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 5 (OOP) — classes, constructors, inheritance, and why composition usually beats inheritance. No AI: model a small library system in classes from a blank file.
Read Phase 11 Chapter 1 (The Pakistani Market). In TARGETS.md, mark which tier each of your fifteen companies sits in and the realistic band.

days.weekTitle: OOP and SOLID — The Shape NestJS Assumes

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 5 — encapsulation, polymorphism, abstract types. Refactor yesterday's library so the storage mechanism can be swapped without touching business logic. That refactor is the whole lesson.
One application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: OOP and SOLID — The Shape NestJS Assumes

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 9 (SOLID) — single responsibility and open/closed. Find the fattest class in your library system and split it. Then add a new storage type without modifying any existing file.
Write a two-minute spoken answer to "how do you decide when to split a class?" using your own refactor as the example.

days.weekTitle: OOP and SOLID — The Shape NestJS Assumes
days.focus: Dependency inversion — the one that matters for Nest

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 9 — dependency inversion. Stop your classes constructing their own dependencies; pass them in. Then, no AI: write a thirty-line container that registers classes by token and resolves their constructor dependencies for you. You have just written the core of Nest.
Second application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: OOP and SOLID — The Shape NestJS Assumes

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 9 — the remaining two principles. These matter least day to day and are still asked. One worked example each, from your own code, in LOG.md.
Third application. Then rehearse: "tell me about a refactor you did and why."

days.weekTitle: OOP and SOLID — The Shape NestJS Assumes
days.focus: Build with your own DI container

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: rebuild the expense tracker from week 3 on your own DI container — a service, a repository interface, two storage implementations, wired by token. When Nest does this for you in week 23, you will know exactly what it is doing.
Drill: three LeetCode problems, timed. Then explain dependency injection aloud in ninety seconds without using the word "framework".
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: OOP and SOLID — The Shape NestJS Assumes
TypeScript for Backend Engineers

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 2 (TypeScript) — basic types, interfaces, type aliases, unions. Set up a project from scratch by hand, no starter template. Read every line of the tsconfig you wrote and know what it does.
One application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: TypeScript for Backend Engineers
days.focus: Strict mode, and what it catches

tasks.text: Turn on strict, strictNullChecks and noImplicitAny. Fix every error the compiler finds instead of silencing it. Write in LOG.md the three real bugs it caught that you would have shipped.
Write a four-sentence answer to "What is TypeScript for?" that does not say "it adds types". Say what problem it removes.

days.weekTitle: TypeScript for Backend Engineers

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 2 — generics and narrowing. No AI: write a typed result wrapper (ok/error) and a typed fetch helper. Ban the word any and feel where it hurts.
Second application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: TypeScript for Backend Engineers
days.focus: Decorators and metadata — the Nest prerequisite

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 2 — decorators. Turn on experimentalDecorators and emitDecoratorMetadata. No AI: write a class decorator, a method decorator and a parameter decorator, and print what each receives. Then use reflect-metadata to read a constructor parameter's type at runtime. That single trick is how Nest injects.
Third application. Then rehearse: "how comfortable are you with TypeScript?" Answer with what you built this week, not a rating.

days.weekTitle: TypeScript for Backend Engineers
days.focus: Functional habits that keep services testable

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 6 (Functional Programming) — pure functions, immutability, side effects at the edges. Pull the pure logic out of one of your services so it can be tested without mocks. This habit is what makes week 27 easy.
Update the CV: TypeScript goes on it now, because you can defend it.

days.weekTitle: TypeScript for Backend Engineers

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: port the expense tracker to strict TypeScript, typed end to end, on your own DI container. Seven weeks of foundations in one piece of code.
Block drill: five LeetCode Easy, timed, no help. Compare directly against your week-1 baseline and write both numbers in BASELINE.md.
BLOCK I REVIEW. Honestly: did the dawn block hold for seven weeks? Did the no-AI rule hold? Unaided problem count now versus week 1? Then read Block II ahead — Node starts.

days.weekTitle: TypeScript for Backend Engineers
The Node Runtime — Modules, npm, Process

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 1 (Node.js) — modules. CommonJS versus ESM, how require actually resolves a path, what each package.json field means. No AI: build a three-module project by hand, both ways, and note what breaks when you mix them.
One application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: The Node Runtime — Modules, npm, Process

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 1 — npm. Semver ranges, the lockfile, dependencies versus devDependencies versus peerDependencies, and what npm ci does differently from npm install. Then read your own lockfile and find one transitive dependency you did not know you had.
Read Phase 10 Chapter 2 (Explaining Technical Work). Explain module resolution aloud, in two minutes, to an imaginary non-engineer. Record it.

days.weekTitle: The Node Runtime — Modules, npm, Process
days.focus: The standard library you never opened

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 1 — fs, path, os, crypto, events. No AI: write a directory-walker that reports total size by file extension. Use path correctly so it works on Windows and Linux. Then use crypto to hash each file and find duplicates.
Second application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: The Node Runtime — Modules, npm, Process
days.focus: EventEmitter, and the pattern Node is built on

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 1 — events. No AI: write your own EventEmitter from a blank file — on, once, emit, off, and correct behaviour when a listener throws. Then read how streams use it.
Third application. Then write five sentences on why Node chose an event-driven model, in the register you would use in an interview.

days.weekTitle: The Node Runtime — Modules, npm, Process

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 1 — process, environment variables, exit codes, uncaught exceptions and unhandled rejections. No AI: write a script that fails properly — non-zero exit, useful message, nothing swallowed. Then make it handle SIGTERM and shut down cleanly.
Update the CV with Node — not as a bullet point but as a sentence about what you built with it this week.

days.weekTitle: The Node Runtime — Modules, npm, Process

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: a file-processing CLI — read a large CSV, filter rows by a flag, aggregate a column, write a report. Flags parsed by hand, no library. Correct exit codes.
Drill: three LeetCode Easy and one Medium, timed, no help. String problems.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: The Node Runtime — Modules, npm, Process
Node Internals — Event Loop Phases, Streams, Buffers

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 1 — the event loop phases: timers, pending callbacks, poll, check, close. Then process.nextTick versus setImmediate versus setTimeout(0). Predict the ordering of a five-line script before running it, and keep predicting until you are right first time.
One application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Node Internals — Event Loop Phases, Streams, Buffers

tasks.text: No AI: write a script that blocks the loop with a synchronous loop and measure the delay it introduces into a timer. Then do the same with a synchronous fs call and with JSON.parse on a huge string. Write the three numbers down — those numbers are an interview answer.
Write a ninety-second spoken answer to "what does it mean that Node is single-threaded?" that is accurate, including the part where it is not.

days.weekTitle: Node Internals — Event Loop Phases, Streams, Buffers

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 1 — libuv's thread pool. Which operations use it (fs, dns, crypto, zlib) and which do not (network I/O). Change UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE and measure the difference on four parallel crypto operations. Most candidates have never done this.
Second application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Node Internals — Event Loop Phases, Streams, Buffers

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 1 — streams. Readable, writable, duplex, transform. No AI: read a large CSV line by line and write a filtered version out without loading the file into memory. Then remove the pipe, write manually, ignore the return value of write(), and watch memory climb. That is backpressure.
Third application. Then explain backpressure aloud in two minutes using what you just watched happen.

days.weekTitle: Node Internals — Event Loop Phases, Streams, Buffers

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 1 — Buffer and binary data. Encodings, why a Buffer is not a string, and what happens when you slice one. No AI: parse a small binary file format by hand — read a header, seek, read records.
Update the CV bullet for Node with something specific from this week — streams, or the thread pool measurement.

days.weekTitle: Node Internals — Event Loop Phases, Streams, Buffers

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: a three-stage stream pipeline — read, transform, write — with a custom Transform stream you wrote, correct error propagation, and a progress report. Run it on a file larger than your available memory.
Drill: three problems, timed. Then explain the event loop phases aloud from memory, in order.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Node Internals — Event Loop Phases, Streams, Buffers
Express — Routing, Middleware, the Request Lifecycle

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 2 (Express.js) — routing, route parameters, query strings, the Router. No AI: build a server with six routes and a mounted router from a blank file. No generator, no template.
One application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Express — Routing, Middleware, the Request Lifecycle

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 2 — middleware. What next() does, what happens when you forget it, and why the order of app.use is load-bearing. No AI: write request-logging and timing middleware by hand, then move one above the other and observe what changes.
Read Phase 9 Chapter 1 (Agile and Scrum). Write how your current team actually works, honestly, and what you would change. You will be asked.

days.weekTitle: Express — Routing, Middleware, the Request Lifecycle

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 2 — the four-argument error middleware and why it has four arguments. No AI: build a central error handler returning consistent JSON that never leaks a stack trace. Then throw from inside an async handler and discover that Express does not catch it — and fix that.
Second application. Then write a ninety-second answer to "walk me through what happens when a request hits your server".

days.weekTitle: Express — Routing, Middleware, the Request Lifecycle

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 2 — body parsing, content types, headers, and status codes that mean what they say. Learn when 400, 401, 403, 404, 409 and 422 are each correct, and set a body size limit before someone finds out you did not.
Third application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Express — Routing, Middleware, the Request Lifecycle

tasks.text: Choose PROJECT 1 and write its scope in one paragraph in PROJECT1.md. It must be a backend you would actually use, small enough to finish, and large enough to need auth, relationships, search and background work. You will carry it for fifteen weeks and rebuild it in Nest in week 23.
Write the one-paragraph description of Project 1 for your CV — present tense, specific, no adjectives.

days.weekTitle: Express — Routing, Middleware, the Request Lifecycle

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: the Project 1 skeleton with a full hand-written middleware stack — request id, logging, timing, body limit, fake auth check, central error handler — each with a comment saying why it sits where it does.
Drill: draw the Express request lifecycle from memory on paper. Then three LeetCode problems, timed.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Express — Routing, Middleware, the Request Lifecycle
REST API Design a Reviewer Would Approve

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 4 (REST APIs) — resources, naming, HTTP verbs, and what "RESTful" actually commits you to. Design the full route table for Project 1 on paper before writing any of it.
One application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: REST API Design a Reviewer Would Approve
days.focus: Status codes and one error shape

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 4 — status codes and error responses. No AI: define your API's error shape once, in writing, then implement it so every error from every endpoint uses it. Consistency here is a reviewer's first impression.
Read Phase 10 Chapter 4 (Written English at Work). Write the Project 1 README — what it is, why it exists, how to run it. Three paragraphs, no filler.

days.weekTitle: REST API Design a Reviewer Would Approve

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 4 — pagination and query design. Offset versus cursor, and why offset pagination gets slower on every page. No AI: implement offset pagination with a maximum page size, then write down what you would change at a million rows.
Second application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: REST API Design a Reviewer Would Approve

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 4 and Chapter 21 (API Versioning) — idempotency, PUT versus PATCH, and versioning strategies. Write in PROJECT1.md which versioning approach you chose and why. An interviewer will ask, and "I did not think about it" is a real answer people give.
Third application. Then rehearse the answer to "how would you version a breaking change without breaking existing clients?"

days.weekTitle: REST API Design a Reviewer Would Approve

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 22 (API Documentation). Document every endpoint by hand first — method, path, parameters, request, response, errors — so you understand the shape. Then generate an OpenAPI document and make it match the implementation exactly.
Put the Project 1 repository link on your CV and LinkedIn now, even though it is not deployed. It is real and it is readable.

days.weekTitle: REST API Design a Reviewer Would Approve

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: Project 1 with two resources, full CRUD, pagination, filtering, consistent errors, in-memory storage. The database arrives in Block III; the shape is what matters today.
Drill: three problems, timed, then explain one solution aloud as if to an interviewer.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: REST API Design a Reviewer Would Approve
Validation, Error Handling, Logging

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 10 (Validation) — schema validation at the edge, and why validating inside the handler is already too late. No AI: add schema validation to every endpoint that accepts a body or a query parameter, and return your standard error shape on failure.
One application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Validation, Error Handling, Logging

tasks.text: Derive your TypeScript types from your validation schemas so they cannot drift apart. Then deliberately change a schema and watch the compiler find every place that assumed the old shape. This is the payoff for week 7.
Write five sentences on what your API does when something goes wrong. If the honest answer is "returns 500", that is this week's work.

days.weekTitle: Validation, Error Handling, Logging
days.focus: An error taxonomy, not a pile of try/catch

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 11 (Error Handling) — operational versus programmer errors, custom error classes, and the boundary where an internal error becomes an HTTP response. No AI: refactor Project 1 onto one taxonomy with a base error class.
Second application, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Validation, Error Handling, Logging

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 12 (Logging) — structured logs, levels, request ids, and what must never be logged (passwords, tokens, personal data). No AI: add a request id that flows through every log line, then trace one request end to end.
Third application. Then rehearse: "a user reports an error from yesterday and gives you a timestamp. What do you do?"

days.weekTitle: Validation, Error Handling, Logging
days.focus: Async context, so ids flow by themselves

tasks.text: Use AsyncLocalStorage so the request id reaches your logger without being passed through every function signature. Understand what it is doing before you use it — this is a genuinely advanced Node feature and a strong interview talking point.
Check APPLICATIONS.md. Anything with no reply after fourteen days is dead — mark it and move on. Do not chase twice.

days.weekTitle: Validation, Error Handling, Logging

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: every endpoint validated, every error on the taxonomy, every log line carrying a request id. Then send ten deliberately malformed requests and confirm every one returns a correct, useful, non-leaking response.
Drill: three problems, timed. Then explain your error taxonomy aloud in two minutes.
Weekly review. Next week the API goes live. Write the deployment checklist tonight. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Validation, Error Handling, Logging
Deploy It — The API Goes Public

tasks.text: Make Project 1 deployable: every secret and every environment difference in environment variables, validated at startup so the process refuses to boot with a missing one. Then check your git history for anything you committed earlier and deal with it honestly.
Two applications, tailored, logged. The quota rises to five a week from today.

days.weekTitle: Deploy It — The API Goes Public

tasks.text: Add a health endpoint that actually verifies the dependencies — not one that returns 200 unconditionally. Learn the difference between liveness and readiness, because it will matter in week 41 when this runs on ECS.
Read Phase 11 Chapter 4 (Referrals and Recruiters). List five people you already know who work at a target company.

days.weekTitle: Deploy It — The API Goes Public
days.focus: Pick a host and read its documentation

tasks.text: Choose a host, create the account, and read its Node deployment documentation end to end before writing anything. Then write your deployment steps down as a checklist. AWS comes in Block VII; today you want it live, not perfect.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Deploy It — The API Goes Public

tasks.text: Handle SIGTERM: stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, close resources, exit zero. Then test it by deploying while making requests and proving nothing was dropped. Most candidates have never thought about this.
Message one referral contact — no ask in the first message, just a real reconnection.

days.weekTitle: Deploy It — The API Goes Public

tasks.text: Rehearse the whole deployment locally against a production-style configuration. Write down every step. It will still fail on Saturday, but it will fail for a reason you can find.
Fifth application of the week. Then prepare the CV line you will use once the URL is live.

days.weekTitle: Deploy It — The API Goes Public

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: DEPLOY. Public URL, HTTPS, environment variables set, health check answering. It will not work the first time. That is the exercise.
Verify from outside: call every endpoint from your phone on mobile data. Then put the URL in the README, on the CV, and on LinkedIn.

Weekly review. Write in LOG.md exactly what broke during the deploy and what you learned from each failure. That list is an interview answer. Read next week ahead — databases, and the most important nine weeks in this plan.

days.weekTitle: Deploy It — The API Goes Public
SQL I — Selects, Joins, Thinking in Sets

tasks.text: Install PostgreSQL locally. Create a practice database with five related tables — customers, orders, order_items, products, categories — and seed a few thousand rows with a script you write yourself. This database is your practice ground for nine weeks.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: SQL I — Selects, Joins, Thinking in Sets

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 1 (SQL) — selection and filtering. Ten exercises by hand. Pay real attention to NULL: why NULL = NULL is not true, what that breaks in a WHERE clause, and why COUNT(column) and COUNT(*) disagree.
Write the difference between WHERE and HAVING in three sentences, as if explaining to a junior.

days.weekTitle: SQL I — Selects, Joins, Thinking in Sets

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 1 — joins. Inner, left, right, full, cross, self. Ten exercises. For each, predict the row count before running it. The prediction is the exercise, not the query.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: SQL I — Selects, Joins, Thinking in Sets

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 1 — GROUP BY, aggregates, HAVING. Ten exercises, at least three needing a join and a group together. That combination is the classic interview question.
Fifth application. Then write the three SQL questions you would ask about your practice schema if you were interviewing yourself.

days.weekTitle: SQL I — Selects, Joins, Thinking in Sets

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 1 — subqueries, correlated subqueries, and common table expressions. Ten exercises. Rewrite three of them both ways and note which reads better and why.
Update the CV: PostgreSQL moves from a listed skill to a sentence about what you did with it.

days.weekTitle: SQL I — Selects, Joins, Thinking in Sets

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: connect Project 1 to PostgreSQL. Replace in-memory storage with real tables and hand-written SQL. No ORM yet, on purpose — you will appreciate it more in week 20.
Drill: five SQL questions, fifteen minutes each, blank editor, no reference. This is exactly the format of a screening test.
Weekly review. Count your forty exercises honestly. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: SQL I — Selects, Joins, Thinking in Sets
SQL II — Window Functions and the Hard Queries

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 1 — window functions. OVER, PARTITION BY, ORDER BY, and how a window differs from a GROUP BY: the rows stay. Six exercises. Say the difference out loud before you move on.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: SQL II — Window Functions and the Hard Queries

tasks.text: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, and the per-group top-N pattern. Six exercises. This exact question — "the three biggest orders for each customer" — is asked constantly and beats most candidates.
Explain the difference between RANK and DENSE_RANK aloud, with an example, in sixty seconds.

days.weekTitle: SQL II — Window Functions and the Hard Queries

tasks.text: Running totals, moving averages, LAG and LEAD, and the frame clause (ROWS versus RANGE). Six exercises. The frame clause is where people who half-know window functions come unstuck.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: SQL II — Window Functions and the Hard Queries

tasks.text: UNION versus UNION ALL, INTERSECT, EXCEPT, and the gaps-and-islands pattern for finding missing sequences and consecutive runs. Six exercises.
Fifth application. Then rehearse: "tell me about the most complex query you have written."

days.weekTitle: SQL II — Window Functions and the Hard Queries

tasks.text: Six exercises against your Project 1 data. Then find two places in Project 1 where you pulled rows into Node and looped over them, and replace each with one query. Write down how many round trips you removed.
Check the funnel: how many replies from your first thirty applications? Under three means the CV is the problem, not the volume.

days.weekTitle: SQL II — Window Functions and the Hard Queries

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: add three reporting endpoints to Project 1 that would have been painful without window functions. All the work happens in the database.
Drill: five SQL questions, timed, blank editor. Include one window function question.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: SQL II — Window Functions and the Hard Queries
Schema Design and Normalization

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 4 (Database Design) — entities, relationships, primary and foreign keys, one-to-many and many-to-many. Redesign the Project 1 schema on paper before touching a migration file.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Schema Design and Normalization

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 5 (Normalization) — first, second and third normal form. Learn each as the anomaly it prevents, not a definition to recite. Then find a table at your current job that violates 3NF and write what could go wrong.
Read Phase 10 Chapter 3 (The Interview Conversation). Note the three things you currently do that the chapter warns against.

days.weekTitle: Schema Design and Normalization

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 4 — constraints. NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, foreign keys, ON DELETE behaviour. No AI: add real constraints to every Project 1 table, then try to insert bad data and watch the database refuse it.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Schema Design and Normalization
days.focus: When to denormalise, and how to say so

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 5 — denormalisation as a trade of write complexity for read speed. Write every one you have chosen into PROJECT1.md with the exact reason. If you cannot write the reason, undo it.
Fifth application. Then practise "how would you design the schema for X" using your own project, ninety seconds, aloud.

days.weekTitle: Schema Design and Normalization

tasks.text: No AI: move the schema into versioned migrations. Write one that adds a column and one that backfills it, then roll both back. A schema you cannot roll back is a schema you cannot change.
Ask one referral contact directly whether they would refer you. Have the CV and a two-line summary ready in the same message.

days.weekTitle: Schema Design and Normalization

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: finish the Project 1 schema — every entity, relationship and constraint, seeded with realistic data by a script you wrote.
Drill: design a normalised schema for a clinic, a courier and a small marketplace. Twenty minutes each, on paper, timed.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Schema Design and Normalization
PostgreSQL in Depth

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 2 (PostgreSQL) — types. timestamptz versus timestamp, numeric versus float for money, text versus varchar, enums, arrays. Fix every wrong type in Project 1 and write down what each one could have cost you.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: PostgreSQL in Depth

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 2 — psql. \dt, \d+, \timing, \x, \ef, and running a file. Stop using a GUI for the rest of the plan. Then inspect your own schema entirely from the command line.
Write a two-minute answer to "why PostgreSQL for this project?" about your project specifically, not a generic comparison.

days.weekTitle: PostgreSQL in Depth
days.focus: JSONB, and when a column is a document

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 2 — JSONB. Operators, containment, and GIN indexes. The honest answer to when it is correct: genuinely schemaless data, not a way to avoid designing a table. Add one justified JSONB column to Project 1, query it, and index it.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: PostgreSQL in Depth

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 2 — CHECK constraints, defaults, generated columns, and partial unique indexes. Push one rule that currently lives in your Node code down into the database, and notice that it is now impossible to violate.
Fifth application. Then rehearse: "where do you put business rules — application or database?" Have a real position and a reason.

days.weekTitle: PostgreSQL in Depth
days.focus: Full-text search, before you reach for Elasticsearch

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 2 — tsvector, tsquery and full-text search. Add search to Project 1 with Postgres alone. Knowing that Postgres can do this is worth an interview answer on its own, because most people add a second system too early.
Update the CV with a specific Postgres line — JSONB, or full-text search, or the type corrections.

days.weekTitle: PostgreSQL in Depth

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: every type correct, constraints in place, search working, JSONB where justified. Then write the data-layer section of PROJECT1.md explaining each decision.
Drill: five SQL and Postgres questions, timed. Then explain JSONB versus a normalised table aloud, with your own example.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: PostgreSQL in Depth
Indexes and Query Plans

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 7 (Indexes) — B-tree structure, and why an index is a trade: faster reads, slower writes, more disk. Look at your tables and predict which columns need indexes before measuring anything. Write the predictions down.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Indexes and Query Plans

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 8 (Query Optimization) — reading a plan. Sequential scan versus index scan, nested loop versus hash versus merge join, and what the cost, rows and actual time numbers mean. Run it on five of your own queries and read every line.
Write a two-minute explanation of what an index is for a non-technical manager, then a ninety-second one for an interviewer. Both aloud.

days.weekTitle: Indexes and Query Plans

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 7 — composite indexes and why column order matters. No AI: create one, then write one query it helps and one it does not, and prove both with EXPLAIN. The left-prefix rule is a standard interview question.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Indexes and Query Plans
