tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 7 — partial indexes, covering indexes and index-only scans, GIN for JSONB and full-text. Add a partial index to Project 1 where most rows are irrelevant, and measure the size difference.
Fifth application. Then rehearse: "this query is slow. Walk me through what you would do." Have an ordered method, not a guess.

days.weekTitle: Indexes and Query Plans
days.focus: The optimisations that are not indexes

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 8 — SELECT *, N+1, unnecessary sorts, functions on indexed columns that disable them, and pagination that degrades. Find at least three of these in your own code and fix them.
Update the CV with a measured number: "reduced X from Nms to Mms". You now have real ones.

days.weekTitle: Indexes and Query Plans

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: index Project 1 properly. Five queries, before and after, EXPLAIN ANALYZE output saved for each. Then write it up — that document is interview material for the rest of the plan.
Drill: five query-plan questions, timed. Read a plan and say what is wrong with it.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Indexes and Query Plans
Transactions and Concurrency — and AI Comes Back
days.focus: AI UNLOCKED — the rules of use

tasks.text: Read the final section of Phase 0 Chapter 4 again. Then write the AI clause into your repository README: I may use AI to review, explain and check, never to author, and I must be able to explain every line here unaided. Eighteen weeks of building the muscle end today; do not undo them in a fortnight.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Transactions and Concurrency — and AI Comes Back

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 6 (Transactions) — ACID. For each letter write your own example from Project 1. A definition you cannot illustrate is one you will fumble in an interview.
Read Phase 10 Chapter 5 (Small Talk and the First Five Minutes). Practise the first ninety seconds of a call aloud — greeting, one line about yourself, one question back.

days.weekTitle: Transactions and Concurrency — and AI Comes Back

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 6 — isolation levels. Dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, and which level permits which. Find out what PostgreSQL actually defaults to and what that means for your code.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Transactions and Concurrency — and AI Comes Back

tasks.text: No AI for this one — do it yourself. Open two psql sessions and deliberately produce a lost update on a Project 1 table. Watch it happen. Write down exactly what each session did and when.
Fifth application. Then rehearse: "how would you handle two users buying the last item at the same time?" You have now actually done it — say so.

days.weekTitle: Transactions and Concurrency — and AI Comes Back

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 6 — locking. Fix yesterday's race three ways: SELECT FOR UPDATE, an optimistic version column, and a single atomic UPDATE. Write the trade-off of each, then choose one for Project 1 and implement it.
Check for any transaction in Project 1 that stays open across a network call. That is a production incident waiting, and finding one is a good interview story.

days.weekTitle: Transactions and Concurrency — and AI Comes Back

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: wrap every multi-step write in a proper transaction, then write a script that hammers one endpoint concurrently and prove the data stays consistent. AI may review what you wrote; it may not write it.
Drill: five SQL questions including two on transactions and deadlocks, timed. No AI — the drill stays AI-free for the rest of the plan, because interviews are.
Weekly review. Honest question: did AI creep back into authoring this week, and where? Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Transactions and Concurrency — and AI Comes Back
ORMs — Prisma and TypeORM
days.focus: What an ORM buys and costs

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 12 (ORMs) — the mapping problem, leaky abstractions, and migration control. Then reproduce an N+1 query deliberately in your own project and measure it. You need to have seen it to talk about it.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: ORMs — Prisma and TypeORM

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 13 (Prisma) — schema definition, the generated client, and migrate. Express the Project 1 schema in Prisma and generate the client. Then read the SQL Prisma actually emits for three of your queries.
Write a ninety-second answer to "ORM or raw SQL?" that refuses the false choice and says when each.

days.weekTitle: ORMs — Prisma and TypeORM
days.focus: TypeORM — because Nest defaults to it

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 14 (TypeORM) — entities, decorators, the repository pattern, relations. Model two Project 1 entities in TypeORM on a branch. You need this specifically for the Nest block, and the decorator work from week 7 is why it will make sense.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: ORMs — Prisma and TypeORM

tasks.text: Port Project 1's queries to Prisma. Keep three in raw SQL on purpose, where the ORM would make them worse, and comment each with the reason. AI may review; it may not write.
Fifth application. Then rehearse: "tell me about a time the ORM was the wrong tool."

days.weekTitle: ORMs — Prisma and TypeORM

tasks.text: Fix your N+1 with eager loading, with a single join query, and with a batched lookup. Measure all three. Then write down which you chose and why — this is a favourite interview question and you now have a real answer.
Update the CV: Prisma and TypeORM both go on now, because you have used both.

days.weekTitle: ORMs — Prisma and TypeORM

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: write your three most complex Project 1 queries both ways and time both against seeded data. Write the comparison into PROJECT1.md with the numbers.
Drill: five questions on ORMs, N+1 and transactions, spoken, timed.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead — NoSQL.

days.weekTitle: ORMs — Prisma and TypeORM
MongoDB and Modelling Without Joins

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 3 (MongoDB) — documents, collections, BSON, and _id. Install it, insert real data, and query it from the shell. Then write down the three things that feel wrong coming from SQL — those instincts are the lesson.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: MongoDB and Modelling Without Joins

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 3 — the central modelling decision. Embed when the data is read together and bounded; reference when it is large, shared, or grows without limit. Model one Project 1 domain both ways and write which you would ship and why.
Write a two-minute answer to "when would you choose MongoDB over PostgreSQL?" An honest "usually I would not, but here is when I would" is a strong answer.

days.weekTitle: MongoDB and Modelling Without Joins

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 3 — aggregation. $match, $group, $project, $sort, $unwind, $lookup. Rewrite three of your SQL reports as pipelines. Notice where $lookup is painful and understand why that is the point.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: MongoDB and Modelling Without Joins
days.focus: Indexes and the explain plan, again

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 3 — indexes in MongoDB, compound index order, and explain(). Everything you learned in week 18 transfers. Prove it: index one slow pipeline and measure the difference.
Fifth application. Then rehearse: "how do transactions work in MongoDB?" — the honest answer includes what changed and what it costs.

days.weekTitle: MongoDB and Modelling Without Joins

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 3 — replica sets, write concern, read preference, and what "eventually consistent" means for your code. This is where NoSQL interview questions actually go, and where most candidates stop.
Update the CV: MongoDB goes on with a sentence about the modelling work, not as a logo.

days.weekTitle: MongoDB and Modelling Without Joins

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: finish the MongoDB version of your domain, get the three pipelines working and indexed, then write the honest comparison in PROJECT1.md — which store, for this project, and why.
Drill: five MongoDB questions, timed, plus one spoken comparison of the two stores.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead — the last database week.

days.weekTitle: MongoDB and Modelling Without Joins
Replication, Partitioning, Sharding — and the Block Close

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 9 (Replication) — primary and replica, synchronous versus asynchronous, and failover. Set up a local replica. Then write to the primary, read immediately from the replica, and see stale data. That is read-after-write, and it is a real interview question.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Replication, Partitioning, Sharding — and the Block Close

tasks.text: Route Project 1's reads to the replica and writes to the primary. Then find the endpoint that breaks because of lag and fix it honestly — read your own writes from the primary. Most people discover this in production.
Write a two-minute answer to "how would you scale reads?" that mentions lag before someone else does.

days.weekTitle: Replication, Partitioning, Sharding — and the Block Close

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 10 (Partitioning) — range and list partitioning, and partition pruning. Partition one large Project 1 table by date, then prove with EXPLAIN that a date-filtered query touches only one partition.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Replication, Partitioning, Sharding — and the Block Close

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 11 (Sharding) — shard keys, cross-shard queries, rebalancing, and why sharding is the answer of last resort. Write down what you would lose in Project 1 if you sharded it today. That list is the answer interviewers want.
Fifth application. Then rehearse the whole scaling ladder aloud: index, cache, replica, partition, shard — in that order, with the reason for each step.

days.weekTitle: Replication, Partitioning, Sharding — and the Block Close

tasks.text: Phase 7 Chapter 7 (Database Scaling) — pull it together. Write the scaling path for Project 1 in PROJECT1.md: what you would do first, second and third as traffic grows, with the signal that would trigger each step.
Rewrite the CV database section from scratch. You have nine weeks of real material and it should read nothing like the October version.

days.weekTitle: Replication, Partitioning, Sharding — and the Block Close

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: finish everything outstanding in the data layer. Then write the data-layer chapter of the README — schema, indexes, transactions, the NoSQL comparison, the scaling path. This document is why you get past screening calls.
Block drill: ten database questions, spoken and written, timed. Compare your comfort against week 14.

BLOCK III REVIEW. Honestly: could I hold a forty-minute database conversation with a tier-2 engineer today? Fifty-plus applications sent — what is the technical-round rate? Then read Block IV ahead — NestJS, and the framework your next job title names.

days.weekTitle: Replication, Partitioning, Sharding — and the Block Close
NestJS Fundamentals — Modules, Controllers, Providers, DI

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 3 (NestJS) — modules. imports, providers, controllers, exports, and what each one means for visibility. Create the Project 2 skeleton by hand with the CLI, then read every generated file and explain it to yourself line by line.
Two applications, tailored, logged. The quota rises to eight a week — you can now hold a database conversation.

days.weekTitle: NestJS Fundamentals — Modules, Controllers, Providers, DI

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 3 — providers and dependency injection. Class providers, useValue, useFactory, useClass, and injection tokens. Then open your week-6 container beside it and write down the four things Nest does that yours did not.
Explain dependency injection aloud in ninety seconds, using your own container as the example and Nest as the grown-up version.

days.weekTitle: NestJS Fundamentals — Modules, Controllers, Providers, DI
days.focus: Controllers as a thin translation layer

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 3 — controllers, routing decorators, and parameter decorators. Build two controllers for Project 2. Keep them thin: parse, delegate, return. If a controller has business logic in it, that logic is in the wrong file.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: NestJS Fundamentals — Modules, Controllers, Providers, DI

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 3 — services and the layering Nest assumes. Controller, service, repository. Move your Project 1 business logic across into services and notice what refuses to move cleanly — that is where Project 1 was badly layered.
Write a two-minute answer to "how do you structure a Nest application?" using your own module graph.

days.weekTitle: NestJS Fundamentals — Modules, Controllers, Providers, DI

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 3 — provider scopes (singleton, request, transient) and why the default is singleton. Then lifecycle hooks, and ConfigModule for environment configuration with schema validation at boot.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: NestJS Fundamentals — Modules, Controllers, Providers, DI

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: Project 2 skeleton — two feature modules, controllers, services, repository interfaces, configuration validated at startup, running and answering. AI may review; it may not write.
Drill: three LeetCode problems, timed, no AI. Then explain the Nest bootstrap sequence aloud from memory.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: NestJS Fundamentals — Modules, Controllers, Providers, DI
The Request Pipeline — Pipes, Guards, Interceptors, Filters

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 3 — the request lifecycle. Middleware, guards, interceptors (before), pipes, handler, interceptors (after), exception filters. Draw it on paper. Then add a console log at every stage and prove the order empirically.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: The Request Pipeline — Pipes, Guards, Interceptors, Filters

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 3 and Chapter 10 — pipes. ValidationPipe, class-validator, class-transformer, and whitelist/forbidNonWhitelisted so unknown fields are rejected rather than ignored. Write DTOs for every Project 2 endpoint and turn validation on globally.
Write five sentences on why validation belongs in a pipe and not in the service.

days.weekTitle: The Request Pipeline — Pipes, Guards, Interceptors, Filters

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 3 — guards and the execution context. Build a role guard using a custom decorator and Reflector metadata — the reflect-metadata work from week 7 is exactly this. Protect one route with it.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: The Request Pipeline — Pipes, Guards, Interceptors, Filters

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 3 — interceptors and the RxJS stream they operate on. Build a logging interceptor that times every request, and a transform interceptor that wraps every response in your standard envelope. You do not need to know RxJS deeply; you do need to know what the observable is.
Rehearse: "what is the difference between a guard, an interceptor and a middleware?" Ninety seconds, with an example of each.

days.weekTitle: The Request Pipeline — Pipes, Guards, Interceptors, Filters

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 3 and Chapter 11 — exception filters. Build a global filter that turns your domain error classes into HTTP responses with the exact error shape you defined in week 11. One taxonomy, two frameworks.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: The Request Pipeline — Pipes, Guards, Interceptors, Filters

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: every DTO validated, one guarded route, timing on every request, one error shape everywhere. Then send ten malformed requests and confirm each returns something correct and non-leaking.
Drill: draw the pipeline from memory, then three LeetCode problems, timed.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: The Request Pipeline — Pipes, Guards, Interceptors, Filters
The Nest Data Layer — TypeORM, Prisma, Transactions

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 14 (TypeORM) with Nest — entities, decorators, relations, and the injected repository. Model the Project 2 schema. Everything you designed in week 16 carries over; only the expression changes.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: The Nest Data Layer — TypeORM, Prisma, Transactions

tasks.text: Generate migrations from your entities, review the SQL they produce line by line, and run them. Then turn synchronize off permanently and write in the README why it must never be true in production. This is a real interview question.
Write a ninety-second answer to "how do you manage schema changes across environments?"

days.weekTitle: The Nest Data Layer — TypeORM, Prisma, Transactions

tasks.text: Put your repositories behind interfaces and inject them by token, so a service depends on an abstraction rather than TypeORM. This is dependency inversion from week 6, and it is what makes week 27's tests easy rather than painful.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: The Nest Data Layer — TypeORM, Prisma, Transactions

tasks.text: Phase 3 Chapter 6 with Nest — transactions. Wrap one multi-step operation spanning two services in a single transaction. Do it the ugly way first (pass the manager through), then with AsyncLocalStorage so it flows invisibly. Compare the two and keep the better one.
Rehearse: "how do you keep two writes consistent when they live in different services?"

days.weekTitle: The Nest Data Layer — TypeORM, Prisma, Transactions

tasks.text: Turn on query logging and read every statement one endpoint produces. Find the N+1 that TypeORM introduced, fix it with a relation load or a query builder, and measure. Week 18 and week 20 both pay off here.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: The Nest Data Layer — TypeORM, Prisma, Transactions

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: Project 2 fully on the database, migrations clean from empty, seeded, indexed, transactional. Then drop the database, run the migrations from scratch, and seed it — if that does not work, it is not finished.
Drill: five questions on ORMs, migrations and transactions, spoken, timed.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: The Nest Data Layer — TypeORM, Prisma, Transactions
Authentication and Authorisation in Nest

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 6 (Authentication) — hashing versus encryption, bcrypt and argon2, salts, and what a work factor is for. Implement registration and login in Nest with hashed passwords and a timing-safe comparison.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Authentication and Authorisation in Nest

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 3 with Passport — the strategy pattern, a local strategy for login, a JWT strategy for requests, and the guards that invoke them. Read the strategy source once: it is a class with a validate method, and that is all.
Write a two-minute answer to "walk me through authentication in your project", including one trade-off you chose and why.

days.weekTitle: Authentication and Authorisation in Nest

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 7 (JWT) — structure, signing, expiry, and the fact that a JWT is signed, not encrypted. Decode one of your own tokens by hand to prove the payload is readable. Then implement refresh with rotation, and answer in writing: how do you actually revoke?
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Authentication and Authorisation in Nest
days.focus: Sessions, and when they are the better answer

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 9 (Session Management) — server-side sessions in Redis, cookie flags (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite), and session fixation. Implement session auth on a branch, then write down which approach Project 2 ships with and why.
Rehearse: "sessions or tokens?" — a candidate with a reasoned answer beats one with a preference.

days.weekTitle: Authentication and Authorisation in Nest

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 8 (OAuth) — the authorisation code flow and PKCE. Add one social login. Then build role-based authorisation with a custom decorator and your Reflector guard, and protect two routes with different roles.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Authentication and Authorisation in Nest

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: finish the auth flow end to end, then attack it yourself — expired token, tampered signature, missing role, reused refresh token, login brute force. Fix everything that gets through.
Drill: five auth questions, spoken, timed. Include "why not localStorage" and "how do you revoke a token".
Weekly review. Read next week ahead — testing, and the chapter the old book did not have.

days.weekTitle: Authentication and Authorisation in Nest
Testing — Unit, Integration, End to End

tasks.text: Phase 9 Chapter 5 (Testing) — the anatomy of a test, arrange/act/assert, and one behaviour per test. Write ten unit tests on the pure business logic in Project 2 — the functions with no database and no HTTP.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Testing — Unit, Integration, End to End
days.focus: Test doubles, and the Nest testing module

tasks.text: Phase 9 Chapter 5 — stubs, mocks, spies and fakes, and when each is honest. Then Nest's Test.createTestingModule: build a module with your repository interface overridden by a fake. Week 25's interfaces are why this is three lines.
Write a ninety-second answer to "what is your approach to testing?" Having a policy, and saying where you stop, beats claiming full coverage.

days.weekTitle: Testing — Unit, Integration, End to End
days.focus: Integration tests against a real database

tasks.text: Phase 9 Chapter 5 — integration testing. A throwaway Postgres in Docker, migrations run before the suite, clean state between tests. Test one repository properly, including the constraint violations you added in week 16.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Testing — Unit, Integration, End to End

tasks.text: Phase 9 Chapter 5 — e2e with supertest against the real Nest application. Test one full journey: register, log in, create, read it back, delete it, confirm it is gone. Then test the unauthorised path for each.
Rehearse: "how would you test this endpoint?" — pick one of your own and answer in three layers.

days.weekTitle: Testing — Unit, Integration, End to End

tasks.text: Write TESTING.md: what gets a unit test, what gets an integration test, what gets e2e, what is not worth testing, and why. Then delete every test you wrote this week that only tests the framework. A policy you can defend is worth more than coverage.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Testing — Unit, Integration, End to End

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: every endpoint covered including one failure path each. Then run the whole suite from a clean checkout and fix whatever only worked on your machine.
Drill: three LeetCode problems, timed, then write tests for one afterwards — some companies interview exactly this way.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Testing — Unit, Integration, End to End
GraphQL and WebSockets in Nest

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 5 (GraphQL) — the type system, queries, mutations, resolvers. Build a code-first GraphQL layer in Nest over one Project 2 module. The decorators will feel familiar now.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: GraphQL and WebSockets in Nest

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 5 — nested resolvers and why they produce N+1 by construction. Reproduce it, watch the query log, then fix it with DataLoader and watch the log again. Two log outputs, before and after, are your interview answer.
Write a two-minute answer to "REST or GraphQL?" that names a concrete situation for each.

days.weekTitle: GraphQL and WebSockets in Nest
days.focus: Errors, auth and limits in GraphQL

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 5 — error handling, guards on resolvers, and query depth and complexity limits. An unbounded GraphQL endpoint is a denial-of-service waiting; add the limits and understand what they compute.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: GraphQL and WebSockets in Nest

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 17 (WebSockets) — the upgrade handshake, and why it is not HTTP after that. Build a Nest gateway that pushes an update when a record changes. Authenticate the connection — most tutorials do not.
Rehearse: "when would you use WebSockets over polling, and when would you not?"

days.weekTitle: GraphQL and WebSockets in Nest

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 17 — what breaks with two server instances: a client connected to instance A never sees an event emitted on instance B. Understand the Redis adapter that fixes it. You will wire it up next week when Redis arrives.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: GraphQL and WebSockets in Nest

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: GraphQL layer working with DataLoader and limits, WebSocket gateway authenticated and pushing live updates. Then document both in the README with the N+1 before-and-after.
Drill: five questions on GraphQL and real-time, spoken, timed.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: GraphQL and WebSockets in Nest
The Work That Happens Later — Uploads, Email, Cron, Microservices
days.focus: File upload, without proxying the bytes

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 13 (File Upload) — multipart, size limits, type validation that checks content rather than the filename, and pre-signed URLs so the file never passes through your API. Implement the pre-signed path.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: The Work That Happens Later — Uploads, Email, Cron, Microservices
days.focus: Email that is not a side effect

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 14 (Email Services) — transactional email, templates, and why sending inside a request handler is wrong. Send it from a queue instead — and if the queue is not there yet, write the interface and fake it until next week.
Write five sentences on what should happen when the email provider is down and a user has just registered.

days.weekTitle: The Work That Happens Later — Uploads, Email, Cron, Microservices

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 15 (Cron Jobs) — the scheduler, cron expressions, and the multi-instance problem: three instances run the job three times. Learn the three fixes — a leader lock, a distributed lock, or a dedicated worker — and implement one.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: The Work That Happens Later — Uploads, Email, Cron, Microservices

tasks.text: Make both scheduled jobs idempotent — running twice must not double anything. Then deliberately run one twice and prove it. This is the discipline that makes queues safe next week.
Rehearse: "your nightly job ran twice and sent duplicate emails. What went wrong and how do you prevent it?"

days.weekTitle: The Work That Happens Later — Uploads, Email, Cron, Microservices

tasks.text: Phase 7 Chapter 9 (Microservices) and Nest's transports. Extract one module into a separate service talking over TCP or Redis. Then write down what you lost: transactions across the boundary, one deploy, easy debugging. That honest list is the interview answer, not enthusiasm. Read Phase 1 Chapter 8 (Design Patterns) alongside it and name the patterns already in your own code.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: The Work That Happens Later — Uploads, Email, Cron, Microservices

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: finish uploads, email, scheduling and the extracted service. Then write the architecture section of the Project 2 README with a diagram.

BLOCK IV REVIEW. Honestly: if someone said "you are a Nest developer", could I defend it for forty minutes? Read Block V ahead.

Redis and Caching Strategies
days.focus: Redis as a data structure server

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 18 (Redis) — strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, TTL. Not "a cache" — a data structure server. Build a leaderboard with a sorted set and a rate counter with a hash, both from the CLI first.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Redis and Caching Strategies

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 19 (Caching) — measure first. Find the most expensive read path in Project 2 with real timings. Write the number down before you cache anything, because the number is what makes this an engineering decision.
Write a ninety-second answer to "how do you decide what to cache?" that starts with measuring.

days.weekTitle: Redis and Caching Strategies

tasks.text: Phase 7 Chapter 3 (Caching) — cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind. Implement cache-aside on your expensive path, measure again, and write both numbers in the README.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Redis and Caching Strategies

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 19 — invalidation. TTL, explicit invalidation on write, and key versioning. Write your strategy down in the README, then deliberately update a record and prove the cache does not serve stale data.
Rehearse: "how do you keep a cache consistent with the database?" An honest answer includes the window where it is not.

days.weekTitle: Redis and Caching Strategies

tasks.text: Phase 7 Chapter 3 — stampede, penetration, avalanche. Simulate a stampede: expire a hot key, fire fifty concurrent requests, and watch fifty identical database queries. Then fix it with a lock or a stale-while-revalidate, and measure.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Redis and Caching Strategies

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: move sessions into Redis, wire the WebSocket Redis adapter from week 28, and confirm two local instances now deliver each other's events. Then check what happens to your app when Redis is down — it should degrade, not die.
Drill: five caching and Redis questions, spoken, timed.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Redis and Caching Strategies
Queues, Workers and Message Brokers

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 16 (Queues) — producers, consumers, and why the worker is a separate process rather than a function. Move email sending onto a BullMQ queue with a real worker. Kill the worker mid-job and see what happens.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Queues, Workers and Message Brokers

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 16 — retry policies, exponential backoff, attempt limits, and the dead-letter queue. Make a job fail deliberately and watch it retry, back off and land in the DLQ. Then build the endpoint that lets you inspect and replay it.
Write a ninety-second answer to "what happens to a job that keeps failing?"

days.weekTitle: Queues, Workers and Message Brokers

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 16 — at-least-once delivery means your consumer will run twice. Make every job idempotent with an idempotency key, then deliver one twice on purpose and prove nothing doubled.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Queues, Workers and Message Brokers

tasks.text: Phase 7 Chapter 4 (Message Brokers) — queues versus topics, RabbitMQ versus Kafka, partitions, consumer groups, ordering guarantees. You will not run Kafka this year; you must be able to say when you would and what it costs.
Rehearse: "RabbitMQ or Kafka?" — answer with the shape of the problem, not a preference.

days.weekTitle: Queues, Workers and Message Brokers

tasks.text: Phase 7 Chapter 5 (Event-Driven Systems) — events versus commands, and the outbox pattern for publishing reliably from a transaction. Make one Project 2 write publish an event that two independent handlers consume.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Queues, Workers and Message Brokers

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: queue, worker, retries, DLQ and the event flow all working. Then push a thousand jobs through and watch the worker keep up or not. Write the throughput number down.
Drill: five queue and messaging questions, spoken, timed.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Queues, Workers and Message Brokers
Rate Limiting, API Gateways and Resilience

tasks.text: Phase 2 Chapter 20 (Rate Limiting) — fixed window, sliding window log, sliding window counter, token bucket, leaky bucket. Implement two by hand against Redis and show the boundary burst problem that fixed windows have.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Rate Limiting, API Gateways and Resilience

tasks.text: Make the limiter correct across instances — the check and increment must be atomic, which means a Lua script or an atomic Redis operation, not a get followed by a set. Then run two instances and prove the limit holds across both.
Write five sentences on why an in-memory rate limiter is wrong behind a load balancer.

days.weekTitle: Rate Limiting, API Gateways and Resilience

tasks.text: Phase 7 Chapter 6 (Distributed Systems) — every network call needs a timeout, and every retry needs a budget and jitter. Add both to every outbound call in Project 2. Then write down what your default timeout is and why that number.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Rate Limiting, API Gateways and Resilience

tasks.text: Phase 7 Chapter 6 — the circuit breaker, its three states, and graceful degradation. Add one around a dependency, then take that dependency down and confirm the service degrades with a useful response instead of hanging.
Rehearse: "a downstream service is slow. What happens to yours?" The answer describes a mechanism, not a hope.

days.weekTitle: Rate Limiting, API Gateways and Resilience

tasks.text: Phase 7 Chapter 8 (API Gateway) — what belongs at the edge: routing, auth, rate limiting, TLS termination. Draw where each concern lives in your architecture, and notice which you have implemented twice.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Rate Limiting, API Gateways and Resilience

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: take down Redis, the database and the email provider one at a time and observe. Fix every case where the service hangs or returns 500 rather than degrading. Write the failure matrix into the README.
Drill: five resilience questions, spoken, timed.
Weekly review. Next week Project 2 ships. Write the checklist tonight. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Rate Limiting, API Gateways and Resilience

tasks.text: Deploy Project 2 — API, worker, Postgres and Redis. The worker is a separate process and must be deployed as one; discovering that today is better than discovering it in week 41.
Two applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Ship Project 2

tasks.text: A live demo with an empty database is a dead demo. Seed realistic data, create a demo account a reviewer can log into, and make every empty state say something useful.

days.weekTitle: Ship Project 2

tasks.text: Read Phase 9 Chapter 2 (Code Reviews and Documentation). Then review Project 2 as someone trying to reject you: dead code, commented-out blocks, secrets in history, TODOs, inconsistent naming, tests that assert nothing. Fix all of it.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Ship Project 2

tasks.text: Collect every measurement you have taken — the index before-and-after, the N+1 fix, the cache hit rate, the queue throughput, the stampede fix — and put them in the README with the method. Measured numbers are what separate your repository from a tutorial.
Record the two-minute demo: the problem, the main journey, one technical decision you are proud of. Re-record until it is clean.

days.weekTitle: Ship Project 2

tasks.text: Final pass: every journey tested on the deployed app from a phone, logged out and logged in. Tag the release.
Three applications. Then rewrite the CV around two shipped services. It should look nothing like the October version — Nest, Postgres, Redis, queues, tests, all defensible.

days.weekTitle: Ship Project 2
days.focus: ANCHOR — Project 2 live, Block V closes

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: whatever is unfinished. If nothing is, write the "what I would do differently" section — reviewers read that one first.
Drill: present both projects back to back, five minutes, as in a first round. Record it and watch it once.

Linux and the Shell

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 1 (Linux) — filesystem layout, users, groups, permissions. Learn what 644 and 755 actually mean and why a private key with the wrong mode is refused. Practise on a real box, not a diagram.
Three applications, tailored, logged. The quota rises to twelve a week — you are now the candidate the CV describes.

days.weekTitle: Linux and the Shell

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 1 — ps, top, kill, lsof, ss, df, du, free. Then answer three questions on a running box: what is listening on port 3000, what is eating memory, what filled the disk.
Write the six steps you would take if a production server stopped responding, in order. This is a real interview question.

days.weekTitle: Linux and the Shell

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 1 — grep, sed, awk, cut, sort, uniq, tail -f, journalctl. No AI: take a raw access log and answer four questions from the command line alone — top endpoints, error rate, slowest paths, busiest hour.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Linux and the Shell

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 2 (Shell Scripting) — variables, conditionals, loops, exit codes, and set -euo pipefail. Write a script that fails loudly instead of continuing quietly, then test every failure path.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Linux and the Shell

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 1 — SSH keys, config and agent. Then cron: schedule your backup script, watch it not run, find out why from the logs, and fix it. Cron failing silently is a rite of passage and a good interview story.
Three applications. Twelve this week.

days.weekTitle: Linux and the Shell

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: a real backup script for Project 2 — dump, compress, timestamp, upload, rotate past seven days, log every step, non-zero exit on failure. Then restore from it, because a backup you have not restored is not a backup.
Drill: three LeetCode problems, timed, no AI. Then one spoken answer on debugging a server you cannot reproduce locally.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Linux and the Shell
Docker and Docker Compose

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 3 (Docker) — images, layers, containers, and the build cache. Write the Dockerfile for your API by hand. Change one line and watch which layers rebuild — that observation is the whole caching lesson.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Docker and Docker Compose

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 3 — multi-stage builds, base image choice, .dockerignore, and running as a non-root user. Get the image under 200MB and write the before and after down.
Read Phase 10 Chapter 11 (Technical English for Engineers). Describe your Docker setup in the register you would use in a pull request.

days.weekTitle: Docker and Docker Compose

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 3 — volumes, networks, port publishing, environment. Then deliberately break container-to-container networking and fix it. That failure is exactly what interviewers ask about.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Docker and Docker Compose

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 4 (Docker Compose) — services, depends_on, healthchecks, named volumes. Bring up API, worker, Postgres and Redis together. Make the database survive a restart and the API wait for it properly.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Docker and Docker Compose

tasks.text: Logs, exec, inspect, and why a container exits immediately. Break your own stack three ways — wrong env var, wrong port, database not ready — and diagnose each from the logs alone.
Three applications. Twelve this week.

days.weekTitle: Docker and Docker Compose

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: finish compose and the README section. Then test the claim — clean clone into a new folder, one command, working stack. More than one command means it is not done.
Drill: three problems, timed. Then explain images versus containers aloud in sixty seconds.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Docker and Docker Compose
Nginx, TLS, DNS and the Network

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 5 (Nginx) and Chapter 12 (Reverse Proxy) — server blocks, location matching, proxy_pass, and the headers a proxy must forward. Put Nginx in front of Project 2 by hand and understand every line you wrote.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Nginx, TLS, DNS and the Network

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 9 (Networking) — TCP handshake, ports, keep-alive, and where latency actually comes from. Then trace a real request with curl -v and dig and write down every step it took.
Write a two-minute answer to "what happens when you type a URL and press enter?" It is the most asked systems question there is.

days.weekTitle: Nginx, TLS, DNS and the Network

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 10 (DNS) — record types, TTL, propagation, and why a low TTL matters before a migration. Point a domain you own at your server and watch the change propagate with dig.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Nginx, TLS, DNS and the Network

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 11 (SSL/TLS) — the handshake, certificates, chains, and what a certificate authority actually asserts. Issue a real certificate with automatic renewal, then confirm renewal works rather than assuming it.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: Nginx, TLS, DNS and the Network

tasks.text: Configure Nginx for what your app actually needs: WebSocket upgrade headers, gzip, client body size for uploads, sensible timeouts, and a rate limit at the edge. Then break each one and see the failure it causes.
Three applications. Twelve this week.

days.weekTitle: Nginx, TLS, DNS and the Network

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: Project 2 live on your own domain over HTTPS behind Nginx. Then write the full request trace into the README — DNS, TCP, TLS, Nginx, Node, Postgres, and back.
Drill: five networking and TLS questions, spoken, timed.
Weekly review. Read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Nginx, TLS, DNS and the Network

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 6 (GitHub Actions) — workflows, jobs, steps, triggers, runners. Write one by hand that installs and lints on every push. Watch it fail, read the log, fix it.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: CI/CD with GitHub Actions
days.focus: Tests in CI with a real database

tasks.text: Add the test job with a Postgres and a Redis service container, migrations, and your week-27 suite. Getting a database to exist in CI is the step that teaches you what your local setup was hiding.
Write five sentences describing your pipeline. It goes in the README and it is an interview answer.

days.weekTitle: CI/CD with GitHub Actions

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 6 — caching dependencies, Docker layer caching, parallel jobs. Get the pipeline under five minutes. A slow pipeline is one people learn to ignore.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: CI/CD with GitHub Actions

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 7 (CI/CD) — secrets, environments, protected deployments, and the principle that CI must never see production credentials it does not need. Move every credential into repository secrets.
Three applications, tailored, logged.

days.weekTitle: CI/CD with GitHub Actions
days.focus: Deploy on merge, and roll back

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 7 — deployment strategies, health-gated deploys and rollback. Wire deployment to run on merge after tests pass. Then break main deliberately, watch the pipeline stop it, and prove the rollback path works.
Three applications. Twelve this week.

days.weekTitle: CI/CD with GitHub Actions

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours: branch protection on main — no direct pushes, required checks, required review. Then work the way a team works for the rest of the plan: branch, PR, review, merge.

days.weekTitle: Jenkins

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 16 — declarative versus scripted pipelines. Write a Jenkinsfile with agent, stages, steps, post conditions and environment. Commit it to the repository — the pipeline is code and lives with the code.

days.weekTitle: Jenkins

tasks.text: Phase 5 Chapter 16 — multibranch pipelines, so every branch and PR builds automatically, and shared libraries, so five repositories do not copy the same eighty lines. Extract one function into a shared library and use it.

tasks.text: Final review, two hours. Read LOG.md from week 1 forward — all fifty weeks. Then write one page: what changed, what did not, what you were wrong about in September 2026, and what you now know you can do.

Write the next eight weeks with dates. With an offer: what you will learn in the first ninety days and the gap you walk in with. Without one: which part of the funnel is failing and what specifically changes — doing the same thing for eight more weeks is not a plan.

THE CLOSE. Three backend services live. Forty problems unaided. Node, Nest, TypeScript, Postgres, Mongo, Redis, queues, Docker, Nginx, CI/CD, Jenkins, AWS, Prometheus and a measured RAG service — all of it built, not listed. Fifty weeks held at fourteen hours a week while employed full-time. Whatever today's offer situation is, the engineer reading this is not the one who wrote BASELINE.md. Write that down, then put the next eight weeks in your calendar.
